nameStory: This tiny crustacean is named after the Hudson River region where it was first scientifically described. The genus name Rhepoxynius comes from Greek words meaning 'current' and 'sharp,' referring to its pointed body shape that helps it navigate water currents.
description: Rhepoxynius hudsoni is a microscopic amphipod crustacean - essentially a tiny shrimp-like creature that's smaller than a grain of rice. These translucent animals typically measure only 2-4 millimeters long and have a laterally compressed (flattened side-to-side) body with multiple pairs of legs. They're part of the diverse world of marine and brackish water invertebrates that most people never notice but play important roles in aquatic ecosystems. **Note: This species is extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation, so identification details should be verified by experts.**

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Flattened from side to side like a tiny transparent pancake, with a distinctly pointed head region that feels firm when gently pressed with a fine probe

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 2-4mm - about the size of a lowercase 'o' in normal book text, requiring magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Nearly completely see-through with a glassy appearance, making internal structures faintly visible like looking through frosted glass

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with rapid, jerky side-to-side motions rather than smooth gliding, creating small water disturbances you can feel if you dip your finger nearby

habitat: Found in brackish waters where rivers meet the sea, particularly in estuarine environments along New England's coast. Look for them in shallow, protected waters with muddy or sandy bottoms where salinity levels fluctuate with tides. They prefer areas with gentle currents and some vegetation or debris for shelter.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures rise and reproduction begins. Look for small clusters in shallow, warming waters of estuaries.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when populations are highest. Best time for observation in tide pools and shallow brackish areas during calm conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still present but beginning to move to deeper waters. May be found among decaying plant matter in protected coves.
seasonality.winter: Least active and hardest to find, typically in deeper water or buried in sediment. Rarely observed during this season.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your pinky nail, these tiny amphipods can leap through the water using their powerful tail-like appendages with such force that they create miniature sonic booms in the water - invisible to us but detectable by sensitive underwater microphones!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny amphipods like Gammarus species, but Rhepoxynius has a much more pointed head and distinctly flattened body profile. Memory trick: 'Rhepoxynius is Really Flat' - the extreme side-to-side compression is the key difference.
contextualKnowledge: **Important note**: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species may be misidentified, extremely rare, or possibly introduced. Any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local marine biologists for verification, as it could represent a significant scientific finding.
compareHints: Since there are no other Rhepoxynius species in our region, compare it to other small phoxocephalid amphipods which tend to be more cylindrical and less dramatically flattened. Rhepoxynius hudsoni's distinctly compressed body shape and sharply pointed head make it unique among New England's amphipod fauna. Most similar species lack the extreme lateral compression that makes this animal look almost leaf-like from the side.
